changeLog.note: Initial original authoring to schema v1.0
Editorial rewrite of advisor and client prose; substance unchanged.

advisor.summary: Above the §199A threshold ($403,500 MFJ / $201,750 single for 2026, with the phase-in range OBBBA widened), a non-SSTB's deduction caps at the greater of 50% of W-2 wages or 25% of wages plus 2.5% of UBIA under §199A(b)(2)(B). When the wage prong binds, raising S-corp owner salary works counterintuitively in the taxpayer's favor: each wage dollar trims QBI by roughly $1.08 after employer FICA yet lifts the cap by fifty cents, so the net deduction keeps growing until the prongs cross near the classic two-sevenths wages-to-profit ratio. The same salary number carries reasonable-compensation exposure from the other direction — Watson stands as the reminder that the floor is enforced — so the target lands inside the defensible comp range, not merely at the mathematical optimum. The engine resets owner wages and prices the full interaction through the deterministic tables, modeling only the 50% wage prong; where UBIA is material, the alternative prong is computed off-model first.
mechanics: Once taxable income clears the threshold plus the phase-in range ($150,000 MFJ / $75,000 single from 2026), the deduction becomes the lesser of 20% of QBI and the greater of 50% of W-2 wages or 25% of wages plus 2.5% of UBIA — §199A(b)(2)(B) supplies the limitation this strategy tunes.

On the wage prong alone, the crossover falls where 20% of (profit minus wages and employer payroll tax) equals 50% of wages — roughly 27-29% of pre-wage profit; below that ratio, each added salary dollar grows the total deduction even as it shrinks QBI.

Every added wage dollar costs employer FICA under §3111 (6.2% up to the Social Security wage base plus 1.45% Medicare, uncapped), and owner wages beyond $200,000/$250,000 pick up the 0.9% additional Medicare tax of §3101(b)(2) — the optimum sits where marginal deduction value equals marginal payroll cost, so the model decides, not a heuristic.

Only W-2 wages properly allocable to QBI and timely reported enter the base, computed under a Rev. Proc. 2019-11 method per Reg. §1.199A-2; guaranteed payments to partners are not W-2 wages and cannot support the limit — this lever belongs to S corporations and entities with genuine employees.
Non-owner payroll counts equally: pulling a planned hire or year-end bonus into the current year raises the cap without adding owner-side Medicare drag.

The engine resets the S corporation's owner wages to the target and reprices the year end-to-end; because it models only the 50%-of-wages prong, capital-heavy businesses should screen the UBIA prong off-model before any salary change.

authority.note: The limitation itself: the greater of 50% of W-2 wages, or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of the UBIA of qualified property.
Defines W-2 wages (properly allocable to QBI, timely reported) and UBIA; excludes guaranteed payments from the wage base.
The three permitted W-2 wage computation methods; whichever is chosen must tie to the W-3/941 filings.
Prices each added wage dollar: employer FICA plus the 0.9% additional Medicare tax that steepens marginal cost above $200k/$250k.

authority.cite: David E. Watson, P.C. v. United States, 668 F.3d 1008 (8th Cir. 2012)
authority.note: The reasonable-compensation floor: artificially low S-corp owner wages get recharacterized — the very salary this strategy tunes upward is bounded below by this line of cases.
The IRS's foundational position that S corporation distributions may be recharacterized as wages for services actually rendered.
Made §199A permanent and widened the phase-in range for 2026 — the thresholds this optimization is calibrated to.

requirements: A non-SSTB S corporation (or an entity with common-law employees) whose deduction is genuinely wage-limited — confirm which constraint binds before touching payroll.
Wages paid and reported within the calendar year on Forms W-2 and 941, tied to a Rev. Proc. 2019-11 computation.
A reasonable-compensation file that supports the chosen salary in both directions.
The UBIA prong screened off-model wherever the business holds substantial qualified property.
risks: Reasonable compensation cuts both ways at exam: David E. Watson, P.C. v. United States, 668 F.3d 1008 (8th Cir. 2012) stands as the warning that artificially low owner wages get recharacterized — and a QBI-driven salary set below the defensible range walks straight into it.
If the deduction is income-limited rather than wage-limited, added salary is pure payroll-tax cost — run the constraint check first.
The engine ignores the UBIA prong; in capital-heavy businesses the 25%-plus-2.5% prong may already lift the cap, leaving added wages a dead cost.
Wages above the additional-Medicare thresholds steepen the marginal cost curve, and state payroll costs and salary-keyed benefit formulas move with the W-2.
An SSTB past the phase-in gets nothing at any wage level — threshold management, not wage tuning, is the SSTB play.
stateNotes: Conformity: most states never adopted §199A, so a wage change plays out at the state level as payroll-tax and withholding mechanics rather than a deduction change.
PTET: shifting profit into wages shrinks the pass-through income base a PTET election taxes — re-run the PTET arithmetic at the new wage level instead of assuming last year's benefit.

Missouri: Missouri's business income deduction (RSMo §143.022) carries no wage limit, so moving profit into wages shrinks the Missouri-side deduction base — a real, if modest, offset to price whenever Missouri is in play; SALT Parity PTET elections (RSMo §143.436) re-price at the new wage split.
reviewChecklist: Binding-constraint analysis in the file: 20% of QBI against 50% of wages (and the UBIA prong where relevant).
Target salary sits inside the documented reasonable-compensation range.
Payroll change executed before December 31, with W-2/941 reporting confirmed.
Additional Medicare tax and state payroll costs built into the marginal math.
PTET arithmetic re-run at the new wage level.

client.teaser: The right salary number can unlock a bigger 20% deduction than you get today.
client.headline: Set your salary to capture the full 20% deduction
plainEnglish: Business owners can deduct up to 20% of their profit. At higher incomes there is a catch: the deduction is capped by how much W-2 payroll the business pays.
Here is the surprise. If the cap is squeezing you, a somewhat bigger salary can raise the cap faster than it shrinks the profit. Done right, the deduction grows even though the salary went up.

There is a sweet spot. Too little salary and the cap chokes the deduction. Too much and payroll taxes eat the gain. We find the exact point for your numbers, test it against a fair-pay standard, and set payroll there.
client.analogy: Your payroll is a hand on a valve, and the deduction is the water flowing through. We open the valve to the exact point where the flow runs strongest without wasting a drop.
benefits: A bigger 20% deduction, often worth thousands each year
Uses a number you already control — no new spending
Doubles as proof for your salary if the IRS ever asks
steps: WE test whether the cap is really limiting your deduction.
WE find the salary level that nets you the most after payroll tax.
YOU approve the change; WE adjust payroll before year-end.
WE re-run the math each year as profit moves.
clientCommitments: Run the approved salary through real payroll before December 31
Tell us about profit swings so the target stays current

annualMaintenance: Re-solve the wage target each year as profit and thresholds move
deliverables: Wage-optimization model showing the marginal math
